<reason>Both sides built coherent, well-structured cases, but A ultimately controlled the two decisive threads better. On the "impossible certainty" charge, B's regress argument (you can't prove recall without releasing) was sharp, but A's answer — testing actual drive strains in large outdoor cages under realistic environmental stress while retaining physical containment — supplied a genuinely achievable middle standard that dissolved the false binary without conceding uncontained release, and A's closing (A5.2) cleanly reframed B's "contradiction" charge as substitution rather than staging. On sovereignty/transboundary consent, A's point that gene flow via mating, wind, trucks, and porous borders outruns any promised "regional consultation" was pressed hard in both rebuttal and closing, and B's answer (confinable constructs die out; consultation is "built into" later stages) never addressed enforcement capacity or the irreversibility-once-mated problem, and was not revisited in B's closing. Since A spoke last in the actual chronology, this sovereignty point stood unanswered at the end, giving A the cleaner final framing. B's mortality-cost weighing and "permanent veto" framing were strong and kept the debate close, but the debate's most concrete, unresolved clash favored A.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's outdoor-cage recall proposal in Rebuttal 2 (A4.1), answering B's "recall requires release" pressure question, was the pivotal exchange: it gave CON an achievable containment standard that survived to the closing, while B's closing contradiction charge (B5.1-B5.3) landed rhetorically but left A's parallel sovereignty/irreversibility argument unrebutted at the end.</best_rebuttal>
